synopsis: Teach-and-Grow Learning (TGL) acquires robot capabilities by modifying an explicit skill library and experience memory while keeping pretrained model weights fixed. An agent organizes semantic subgoals, delegates motion to robot executors, checks outcomes, and revises the remaining route [E03–E08]. The strongest controlled comparison adds two blocks to a fixed executor and improves simulated LIBERO success from 0/6 to 4/6. This supports a small-scale capability-growth mechanism; the proposed lifetime scaling law and fast-policy distillation remain untested extensions [E09–E11, E15].

problem.text: The authors identify a mismatch between local deployment failures and globally coupled policy updates: an unfamiliar object, contact condition, sensor, or embodiment can require additional interaction data, optimization, and regression testing. TGL proposes independently inspectable and locally validated capability additions as a way to reduce this recurring retraining burden.

contributions.text: An agent-centered acquisition and execution architecture separates fixed pretrained parameters from an evolving library of executable behaviors and structured experience.
Skill Blocks express reusable semantic effects through explicit scope, grounding, executor, verification, and recovery contracts. Their physical realization is recomputed for the current scene.
Controlled LIBERO studies demonstrate block induction, save-and-reload persistence, feedback-dependent routing, and a fixed-executor library expansion.
The paper proposes power-law decreases in future-task error and teaching demand as effective reusable experience accumulates, together with a longitudinal testing protocol.

inputs: Task instruction and sparse successful teaching trajectories or visual demonstrations [E03, E06, E13, E14]
Fresh agent-view and wrist observations, grounding evidence, and robot state [E12, E20]
Registered Skill Blocks, structured Experience Memory, permitted executors, and verifier or planner evidence [E04, E05, E12]
outputs: A revisable sequence of semantic behaviors and robot actions executed by block-specific backends [E04, E08, E20]
Observed pass, fail, or inconclusive block outcomes [E04, E08]
Validated library additions and persistent records of context, failures, and repairs [E03, E05, E21]

steps.name: Extract shared task structure
steps.detail: Divide demonstrations around meaningful state changes and align segments by achieved effect rather than timing or motor coordinates. Preserve object roles, relations, ordering, and reusable strategy; leave pose, grasp, path, and controller commands for runtime grounding.

steps.name: Construct a scoped behavior contract
steps.detail: Represent each block as ⟨g, S, ρ, γ, Π, v, R⟩: intended effect, applicability scope, strategy, observation-to-variable grounding, compatible executors, outcome verifier, and bounded recoveries. The demonstrated acquisition block remains specific to the alphabet-soup can; its contract requires verified retention and displacement.

steps.name: Ground and execute locally
steps.detail: Bind the selected block to fresh scene evidence. The current stack uses detection, segmentation, RGB-D, and robot state for grounding; Contact-GraspNet and MPLib provide grasps and collision-aware motion, with bounded controllers executing local actions.

steps.name: Revise the route from outcomes
steps.detail: Run one semantic stage and return observations plus executor/verifier evidence to the agent. The agent may continue, gather evidence, change executor, recompose the remaining blocks, request teaching, or stop. Continuous motor control stays inside the executor.

steps.name: Validate and preserve the lesson
steps.detail: Test candidate blocks on separated cases and narrow unsupported scopes before admission. Store executable behavior in the library and task context, outcomes, diagnoses, repairs, and evidence in memory. Retrieval, grounding, and behavioral retention require checks beyond merely saving the block.

training.text: Task acquisition updates explicit skill, memory, and history state while foundation parameters θ remain fixed. Demonstrations supply structural evidence rather than supervised targets for task-specific policy optimization.

The reported visual decomposition study uses a deterministic procedure. Multimodal-agent decomposition and cross-demonstration synthesis describe the broader formulation and should not be attributed wholesale to the measured visual study.
Training a separate fast student with parameters ϕ from verified trajectories is proposed as later compression. The paper does not report an implemented distillation experiment.

inference.text: The online traces use gpt-5.6-sol, seed 0, structured decisions, at most one evidence refresh, and two replans. The agent receives registered blocks and allowed tool routes; humans do not modify in-episode decisions.

The demonstrated control mechanism is semantic routing with observed feedback. Learned future-state prediction is optional in the wider architecture; no joint future-video/action predictor or inverse-dynamics action extractor is specified as the evaluated mechanism.

equations.explanation: Equation (3) identifies the learned state: teaching D_n and useful execution lessons ΔH_n update the library B and memory M through U, while pretrained weights remain unchanged and history H accumulates evidence.
Equation (10) executes the first block of the current working plan with a selected compatible executor π. The returned observation and outcome evidence ε determine the next semantic decision.

equations.expression: X_n = Σ_{h∈H_n} ω(h; B_n, M_n); E_future(X) = E_∞ + A X^(−α); D_teach(X) = D_∞ + B X^(−β).
equations.explanation: Equations (7) and (1) define the proposed scaling resource and response curves. Each checkpoint-only weight ω lies in [0,1] and considers reliability, coverage, retrieval, grounding, and compatibility without future outcomes. X is positive; floors are nonnegative and coefficients/exponents positive. D_teach is intervention time under a fixed success criterion and capped budget. No curve is fitted in the reported experiments.

results.setting: Ten successful demonstrations from two LIBERO-Object condiment-transfer tasks, five per task. Production inputs exclude actions, hidden object state, rewards, task-success labels, and reference boundaries; annotations are used afterward.
results.metric: Ordered role/type accuracy; boundary F1; observable effect confirmations
results.value: 40 predicted and 40 reference stages; accuracy 1.000; boundary F1 0.100 exact, 0.633 within one sampled frame, and 0.900 within two; 20/20 effects confirmed.
results.comparison: Reference annotations and observable acquisition/release tests; no competing decomposition method reported.
results.interpretation: Semantic role recognition is stronger than exact temporal localization. These are demonstration-analysis measurements, not newly executed task success.

results.setting: Three teacher trajectories from states 0–2; evaluation on separated states 3–5; additional scope testing on states 6–8.
results.metric: Simulated task successes before and after library serialization
results.value: Learned two-block route: 3/3, and 3/3 after save-and-reload.
results.comparison: The existing six-block route also succeeds on 3/3 of the same evaluation states.
results.interpretation: The learned route becomes a persistent alternative, without improving success over the old route on this split. It stops at unmet semantic effects on farther states; these stops establish scope enforcement, not successful generalization there.

results.setting: Two LIBERO-Object tasks; onboarding states 12–14; matched disjoint evaluation states 15–17. Executor, runtime, seed 0, success criteria, and three-attempt budget are fixed; library contents and scopes are frozen before evaluation.
results.metric: Evaluation success; 95% Wilson intervals; two-sided Fisher exact test
results.value: Eight blocks: 4/6, interval [0.30, 0.90]; six blocks: 0/6, interval [0.00, 0.39]; p = 0.061.
results.comparison: Only the learned acquisition and release blocks are added.
results.interpretation: The comparison supports a local library-growth mechanism under a fixed executor. Two tasks, one seed, and broad intervals limit claims of general superiority.

results.task: Acquisition effort in the fixed-executor pilot
results.setting: Same two-task pilot; unsuccessful acquisitions remain counted at the three-attempt cap.
results.value: 1.5 with eight blocks versus 2.5 with six blocks.
results.comparison: Expanded versus original library under the fixed budget.
results.interpretation: This is a capped attempt-count result. It does not measure teacher intervention time or validate the proposed teaching-demand scaling curve.

results.setting: Two representative successful traces selected from a frozen LIBERO-GOAL archive.
results.metric: Qualitative workflow changes after physical feedback
results.value: Bowl-on-plate: remaining route rebuilt after grasp evidence proves insufficient for placement. Drawer opening: inconclusive evidence triggers a fresh observation.
results.comparison: The initial route or observation state within each trace; no matched fixed-workflow ablation.
results.interpretation: The traces show that feedback can change agent decisions, but their selection does not establish a success rate or causal performance gain.

results.value: 0/8 successes; two failures before motion planning, four involving path consistency or calibration, and two involving gripper closure.
results.comparison: No repaired-system baseline reported for this cohort.
results.interpretation: The system provides localized failure descriptions, while this cohort also exposes unresolved execution weaknesses. It must not be pooled with the library pilot.

limitations.text: The paper asserts state-of-the-art standard LIBERO performance, but the supplied results contain no suite-level scores, competing-method table, or standard evaluation protocol sufficient to verify that assertion.
Sequential agent reasoning, observation, and tool use make unfamiliar-task execution slow. Faster models and distillation are proposed remedies; no latency measurements establish their benefit.
The evaluated studies use LIBERO simulation and one embodiment. They do not establish physical deployment reliability, cross-embodiment transfer, or broad continual-learning retention.

Persistent files avoid direct parameter overwriting, but harmful retrieval, invalid grounding, or executor changes can still degrade behavior. Repeating three evaluation states after reload is a limited retention test.

Lifetime power laws and near-additive acquisition cost are hypotheses. The latter requires bounded local teaching, grounding, validation, and linking costs plus at-most-linear cumulative retrieval cost; unrestricted compatibility checks could defeat that condition.

reproduction.text: Reconstruction requires the agent configuration, exact LIBERO task identifiers and versions, six-block baseline library, induction procedure, Contact-GraspNet/MPLib configurations, calibration, controller parameters, prompts, and verifier thresholds. The supplied text names components and splits but does not provide all implementation details. No code was inspected and no experiments were reproduced for this report.

The smallest useful mechanism test is the matched six-versus-eight-block pilot: preserve the published onboarding/evaluation separation, freeze all other components and budgets, and log block selection and verified outcomes. Additional seeds and old-task evaluations would test whether the improvement persists beyond the reported cells.

Testing lifetime scaling additionally requires an operational, preregistered experience-weighting rule, fixed models/tools/inference budgets, intervention-time measurements, and held-out later checkpoints. The paper specifies this design but supplies neither fitted exponents nor an instantiated numerical weighting rule.

reasoning.text: The foundational-work placement and not-applicable WAM architecture/prediction/quadrant fields fit a system architecture centered on planning, explicit capability updates, and verification. Its current agent and robot executors are separate components; WAMs are optional executors, future students, or planning aids. The paper does not introduce a joint future/action prediction architecture or inverse-dynamics mechanism requiring a WAM quadrant. The broad technical-resource subcategory is compatible with this role, although the resource itself is an architecture paper with experiments, not a survey.

discussionQuestions: Can agent-based induction reproduce the deterministic visual study's semantic accuracy while improving exact boundary localization [E13]?
How much of the library pilot's gain comes from the new executable strategies versus their grounding, scope, and verifier definitions [E07, E15]?
Can experience weighting predict held-out future-task gains without being tuned to those outcomes, and do power laws outperform alternative curves [E10, E11]?
How do retrieval and behavioral retention change as the library grows far beyond the tested eight blocks [E15, E19]?

evidence.location: PDF p. 1, title, author list, and arXiv version line
evidence.detail: The title and authors Chang Nie, Zhe Liu, and Hesheng Wang match the catalog; the page identifies arXiv:2608.17209v1 and 17 August 2026.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 1–3, Section I; p. 10, Appendix A.C–D
evidence.detail: The authors frame retraining tax as collection, policy updating, and regression testing caused by uncovered physical conditions, and propose local Skill Block integration as an alternative update unit.

evidence.location: PDF p. 4, Section III.A, Eqs. (2)–(3)
evidence.detail: Sparse teaching and execution lessons update the Skill Library, Experience Memory, and history while foundation parameters θ remain fixed; a later student has separate parameters ϕ.

evidence.location: PDF p. 4, Section III.B, Eqs. (4)–(5)
evidence.detail: Seven block fields specify goal, scope, strategy, grounding, executor choices, three-valued verification, and recovery. The ordered working plan can change after a block outcome.

evidence.location: PDF p. 4, Section III.C, Eq. (6); p. 13, Appendix F.B
evidence.detail: Memory records task, context, blocks, outcome, diagnosis, repair, and evidence. Records guide later choices and remain inspectable; executable behavior resides separately in blocks.

evidence.location: PDF p. 5, Section IV.A, Eqs. (8)–(9)
evidence.detail: Demonstrations are segmented at semantic state changes, aligned by effect, and synthesized into shared strategy while scene-dependent physical quantities are recomputed.

evidence.location: PDF p. 13, Table III, Scope, Strategy, Grounding, Executors, Outcome test, Recovery, and Excluded rows
evidence.detail: The acquisition block is specific to the alphabet-soup can. It uses fresh grounding, grasp selection, servo acquisition, collision-aware transitions, and retention/displacement verification; stored demonstration coordinates and action replay are excluded.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 5–6, Sections IV.B–D, especially Eq. (10)
evidence.detail: The agent selects compatible executors and receives new observations plus outcome evidence after block execution. Semantic decisions can change evidence acquisition, executor, route, teaching request, or stopping, while motor control remains delegated.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Section IV.E; p. 8, Section VI.E; p. 16, Appendix H.D
evidence.detail: Verified agent trajectories are proposed as training data for a fast policy; unfamiliar or uncertain situations return to the agent. Distillation is presented as a future extension.

evidence.location: PDF p. 3, Eq. (1); pp. 4–5, Section III.D, Eq. (7)
evidence.detail: Effective experience sums weights in [0,1] using checkpoint evidence without future outcomes. Proposed power laws relate positive experience to future error and capped teacher-intervention time, with nonnegative floors and positive coefficients/exponents.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 14–15, Appendix G.C–E, Eqs. (15)–(16)
evidence.detail: Near-linear cumulative TGL cost depends on bounded local block costs and at-most-linear retrieval. The proposed longitudinal study fixes resources, evaluates multiple task types, retains capped acquisitions, and tests curve predictions on later held-out checkpoints.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Section V.b; p. 17, Appendix I.A
evidence.detail: Two selected successful LIBERO-GOAL traces show bowl-on-plate route rebuilding and drawer-opening reobservation. Configuration is gpt-5.6-sol, seed 0, structured decisions, one evidence refresh and two replans maximum, without human in-episode edits.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Section V.a; p. 17, Appendix I.B
evidence.detail: The visual study is deterministic and uses ten demonstrations, five per related condiment-transfer task. It reports 40 predicted/reference stages, role/type accuracy 1.000, boundary F1 0.100/0.633/0.900 at exact/one-frame/two-frame tolerances, and ten acquisition plus ten release confirmations. Restricted production inputs and post-prediction annotation are specified.

evidence.location: PDF p. 17, Appendix I.C; p. 7, Table I, Task-specific learning cycle row
evidence.detail: Teaching states 0–2 produce two blocks; both learned and existing routes succeed on states 3–5 at 3/3. The learned route repeats 3/3 after reload and stops at missing semantic effects on states 6–8.

evidence.location: PDF p. 17, Appendix I.D; p. 7, Table I, Fixed-executor library pilot row
evidence.detail: The two-task, seed-0 pilot freezes executor, runtime, success criteria, three-attempt budget, and pre-evaluation library scopes. Onboarding uses states 12–14 and evaluation 15–17. Six/eight blocks yield 0/6 versus 4/6, Wilson intervals [0.00,0.39]/[0.30,0.90], Fisher p=0.061, and capped median attempts 2.5/1.5.

evidence.location: PDF p. 17, Appendix I.E
evidence.detail: A separate cohort has zero successes in eight acquisition attempts: two failures before motion planning, four involving path consistency or calibration, and two at gripper closure.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, opening of Section V; p. 7, Table I; p. 17, Appendix I
evidence.detail: Section V asserts state-of-the-art standard LIBERO success. Table I and Appendix I instead present controlled decomposition, learning, trace, pilot, and failure-cohort results, without a standard-suite score or competing-method comparison.

evidence.location: PDF p. 8, Section VI.F; pp. 11–12, Appendix C.C
evidence.detail: The authors identify multiple sequential agent calls, tool operations, and observations as a practical time cost, and anticipate model, caching, and fast-student improvements.

evidence.location: PDF p. 13, Appendix F.C, Four Levels of Retention
evidence.detail: Storage, retrieval, grounding, and behavioral retention are distinct. The paper explicitly cautions that persistent storage alone does not establish preserved competence.

evidence.location: PDF p. 17, Appendix J, Current System
evidence.detail: The current stack combines a multimodal coding agent, visual analysis, detection/segmentation, RGB-D and robot state, Contact-GraspNet, MPLib, bounded controllers, fresh effect checks, and persistent stores. WAM execution and distillation are described as possible replacements or next steps.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 12–13, Appendix E.C–F
evidence.detail: Alignment separates semantic and behavioral invariants from instance variables. Scope broadens only with supporting variation, and candidate blocks are tested on separated cases. The present study uses one embodiment; cross-embodiment reuse is a future test.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 15–16, Appendix H.B–D
evidence.detail: VLAs and WAMs may execute blocks or mature compositions, or serve as distilled students. World models may screen alternatives. Semantic contracts let the agent organize learned and classical components without prescribing one predictive model.
